name: The Joule-Thomson Effect
statement: Let a real gas expand through a valve without adding heat, and most gases cool.
meaning: The Joule-Thomson effect is the temperature change a real gas or liquid undergoes when it is forced through a valve or porous plug while thermally insulated, so no heat is exchanged with the surroundings. This throttling happens at constant enthalpy, and for most gases at ordinary temperatures it produces cooling, though a few, notably hydrogen and helium, warm instead. The effect is the basis of gas liquefaction and much of refrigeration, and it is intrinsically a real-gas phenomenon: an ideal gas, with no forces between its molecules, shows no Joule-Thomson temperature change at all. Studied by James Joule and William Thomson in the 1850s, it is a cornerstone of low-temperature physics and cryogenic engineering.
mechanism: As a real gas expands through the throttle, its molecules move farther apart, and because real molecules attract one another, work must be done against those attractions. That work draws on the gas's own internal energy, and since no heat enters, the temperature falls. Whether a gas cools or warms depends on its Joule-Thomson coefficient, which changes sign at a temperature called the inversion temperature: below it the gas cools on expansion, above it the gas warms. Hydrogen and helium have inversion temperatures below room temperature, so they warm when throttled at ordinary conditions and must be pre-cooled before throttling will cool them. An ideal gas, having no intermolecular forces, does no such work and its temperature is unchanged, since its enthalpy depends only on temperature.

examples.text: Repeated throttling and cooling in the Linde process liquefies air, producing liquid nitrogen and oxygen, a direct industrial use of the Joule-Thomson effect.
Because their inversion temperatures are low, hydrogen and helium heat up on throttling at room temperature and must be pre-cooled before the effect will cool them.

examples.tag: No effect for an ideal gas
examples.text: An ideal gas, lacking intermolecular forces, shows no temperature change on throttling, so the effect is a genuine signature of real-gas behaviour.

variants.name: The inversion temperature
variants.text: The temperature at which a gas's Joule-Thomson coefficient changes sign, separating the regime where throttling cools it from the regime where it warms.

variants.name: The Linde liquefaction cycle
variants.text: The industrial process that uses repeated Joule-Thomson expansion, with pre-cooling, to liquefy air and other gases including nitrogen and oxygen.

whyItMatters: The Joule-Thomson effect is a cornerstone of cryogenics and industrial gas processing, the physical basis for liquefying air and other gases and for much of refrigeration. The Linde process, built on repeated throttling and cooling, produces the liquid nitrogen, oxygen, and argon on which industry, medicine, and science depend, and pre-cooled versions reach the extreme cold needed to liquefy hydrogen and helium for superconductors and space technology. As a clear manifestation of intermolecular forces and real-gas thermodynamics, the effect also sharpens the distinction between ideal and real gases, making it both practically vital and conceptually instructive.

working.text: force a real gas through a valve or plug while insulated so no heat enters, changing its temperature at constant enthalpy.
expect cooling below the gas's inversion temperature and warming above it, which is why hydrogen and helium warm at room temperature.
repeat expansion and cooling, as in the Linde cycle, to drive a gas down to liquefaction, pre-cooling those with low inversion temperatures.

limits: The effect is a real-gas phenomenon; an ideal gas shows none, so it depends on intermolecular forces and vanishes in their absence. Not all gases cool on throttling: whether a gas cools or warms depends on being below or above its inversion temperature, so hydrogen and helium warm at room temperature. The process is isenthalpic, at constant enthalpy, not constant temperature, and is irreversible. The cooling per expansion is modest, so liquefaction requires repeated cycling and often pre-cooling, and the effect operates within the limits set by each gas's inversion temperature and thermodynamic properties.
misreadings: The Joule-Thomson effect is not universal cooling; hydrogen and helium warm when throttled at room temperature because their inversion temperatures lie below it. It is a real-gas effect and disappears entirely for an ideal gas, so it cannot be derived from ideal-gas assumptions. And it occurs at constant enthalpy, not constant temperature or in a vacuum-free expansion; it is throttling through a resistance, distinct from the free expansion of a gas into a vacuum, which for an ideal gas also produces no temperature change but by a different argument.
origin: Investigated by James Prescott Joule and William Thomson, Lord Kelvin, in a series of experiments around 1852, and later made the basis of the Linde process for liquefying gases.
